summary: Describes a general architecture for a reputation service, where reputation means predictions about an entity or identifier such as a domain name, following the protocol model recommendations of RFC 4101. This is an architecture document that later documents build on.

eli5.summary: A way to ask a trusted friend whether a name is trustworthy.

subtitle: A general design for asking a service how trustworthy a domain name or other identifier is.

tldr.problem: Authentication such as DKIM proves who is using a name but not whether that actor is good or bad, so there is no common way to ask for an assessment of an identifier.
tldr.mechanism: A client extracts an identifier from content, asks a reputation service about it in a given Application context, and gets back a Response Set holding an assertion and a rating. The query and response are generic and extended per application.
tldr.outcome: It supplies the vocabulary and model that RFC 7071, RFC 7072 and RFC 7073 build on, while leaving data collection and rating methods out of scope.

today: RFC 7070 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 2013, and the data lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The concrete formats and protocol are in RFC 7071, RFC 7072 and RFC 7073.

sections.title: Why Reputation Is Needed
sections.content:
Many Internet protocols work between unauthenticated parties. The email From: field can hold any display name or address, and an SMTP server trusts that the DNS led it to the right receiver. This makes spam and phishing easier.

Mechanisms such as DKIM now bind a validated identifier to a message, but that does not separate good actors from bad. The RFC notes that bad actors tend to adopt such mechanisms even faster, hoping receivers will confuse identity authentication with identity assessment. The former only says the name is used by its owner or agent. The latter says something about the owner's quality.

The RFC defines reputation as the estimation in which an identifiable actor is held, especially by the community or the Internet public generally. It is not limited to email. It could rate web site security, an ISP, or e-commerce customer satisfaction.
sections.eli5: A stranger can wear a name tag that says 'Nice Guy', and the tag proves it is really his tag. It does not prove he is nice, so you want to ask people who know him.

sections.title: Overview and Scope
sections.content:
The premise is a client that wants to evaluate content using an identifier tied to it, and a reputation service provider that collects, aggregates and offers scores. Client and provider operators typically agree beforehand on where the service is reached, what data is offered, and possibly client authentication details.

On receiving content, the client extracts identifiers, such as the domain in the From: field or the domain from a valid DKIM signature. It queries the service with the identifier and possibly context or client-specific information, then folds the answer into its own local logic to decide what to do with the content.

The architecture defines only the query and a basic response format, allowing extensions per application. How a reputation agent collects data or computes an evaluation is explicitly out of scope. The RFC likens the difference between a basic rating and underlying detail to check approval versus a credit report.
sections.eli5: You read a name on a letter, ask a trusted helper about it, and then decide for yourself whether to open the letter.

sections.title: High-Level Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture defines vocabulary, the types and content of supported queries, an extensible range of response information, and query and response transport conventions. It is a simple query and response model that can run over several transports, including the DNS, much as a DNS BlockList does. Each transport specification is independent. The exact syntax of queries and responses is defined by each application.

The companion documents are RFC 7071 (a media type and serialization for responses, plus the registry for contexts), RFC 7072 (a query protocol over HTTP) and RFC 7073 (a first application: email identifiers).

The worked email example has a Sender, MSA, MTA path to the receiving MTA, where an Identifier Verifier (DKIM) passes validated domain names to an Identifier Assessor. The assessor queries a Reputation Service and hands identifiers and their reputations to a Handling Filter, which decides whether and how the Recipient's MDA delivers the message, possibly using other inputs too.
sections.eli5: A mail room checks who a package claims to be from, asks a rating helper about that sender, and then a sorter decides whether to deliver it.

sections.title: Applications, Response Sets and Reputons
sections.content:
An Application is a specific context in which reputation queries are made, such as restaurants, movies or email senders. Each has its own attributes of interest, so each must be formally defined. Names and their specifying documents are registered with IANA in the "Reputation Applications" registry, created by RFC 7071.

A Response Set is the data returned about an entity within an Application. It always has the name of the entity, the Assertion and the Rating. The rest is application specific.

An Assertion is a claim about the subject, such as 'serves good food'. Its Rating says how much the responder agrees, typically a floating point value from 0.0 (no support) to 1.0 (total agreement). Application specifications fix the scale so a client can switch providers or aggregate several, for instance by stating that ratings are linear. A reputon is the object that carries the Response Set in serialized form; its encoding is left to other documents.
sections.eli5: A rating is like stars given for one claim, such as 'good pizza', from none at all to full. Everyone using the same star scale means scores from different helpers can be compared.

sections.title: Information in the Protocol
sections.content:
Whatever the transport, a query normally includes the subject, the name of the reputation context (the Application), and optionally the names of the specific assertions of interest. Some transports or contexts may need more parameters.

A response normally includes the identity of the entity providing the information, the identity of the entity rated, the application context, and the overall rating. Further data may be included for specific uses. For example, a Response Set for an 'email-sending-domain' might say how often spam was received from that domain.

The basic Response Set could be wrapped in a MIME media type or a DNS resource record, or be the payload of a purpose-built protocol. In the basic scenario one entity (the client) asks a second (the server) about a third (the subject). Some applications want a very lightweight mechanism, others larger and more complex responses.
sections.eli5: You ask 'how is this shop at pizza?' and the answer says who is answering, which shop, which topic, and the score.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Reputation exchanges can be sensitive. A client reveals which subjects it cares about, and in email, from whom it receives mail. A server reveals what its sources report. This matters most across administrative domains, and some information (a credit rating) is more damaging to leak than other (movie ratings).

The RFC says DNS queries and responses are entirely insecure, so sensitive data needs a transport with adequate security. It very strongly advises HTTP over TLS, and for email advises OpenPGP and S/MIME. Aggregated output and stored inputs also need protection.

Queries can also leak: a provider can infer a subject exists and watch who asks about it. If client credentials are compromised, the main exposure falls on the third party whose reputation is revealed.
sections.eli5: Asking about someone tells the helper whom you are curious about, and the helper's answers are private opinions. Both should be kept in sealed envelopes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This is a high-level architecture with no implementation details, so the analysis is high level too. A client places trust that a service gives an unbiased opinion. A biased service could let spam, phishing or malware through by rating a domain too favorably, or cause needless rejection or delay by rating it too harshly. A compromised service, or a man-in-the-middle, could return biased results too. A suggested mitigation is to use services that disclose how they compute results, though that is out of scope.

Clients and servers also need to resist malformed messages, which can confound identification of the responsible party. Finally, involving a third party that can influence handling of incoming content means ceding some control to it.
sections.eli5: If your helper lies or gets tricked, you can be misled, so you should pick helpers you trust and be careful with strange or broken messages.

messages.label: Query: subject + Application
messages.note: Optionally names the assertions of interest.

items.title: Application
items.text: The context of a query, such as email senders or movies.

items.title: Response Set
items.text: Entity name, Assertion and Rating, plus application-specific data.

items.title: Assertion
items.text: A claim about the subject, such as 'serves good food'.

items.title: Rating
items.text: Agreement with the assertion, typically 0.0 to 1.0.
